molarity-from-stock.formula: stock_M = 10 x purity_pct x density / MW (mol/L); volume_to_draw = target_M x final_volume / stock_M (mL).
molarity-from-stock.edition: Standard reagent preparation - stock molarity from assay and density, by name.
molarity-from-stock.freeAccess: Standard analytical-chemistry reagent-preparation relation; the reagent lot certificate of analysis governs.
molarity-from-stock.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
molarity-from-stock.editionNote: A concentrated liquid reagent is labeled by weight percent and density, not molarity, so both must be combined with the molecular weight (ignoring the density is a 15-45% error on common acids; ignoring the assay percent is far larger); the 10 factor converts g per 100 mL to per liter. Always add concentrated acid to water, never the reverse. A prep aid, not a substitute for the certificate of analysis.

assumptions.name: Assay and density
assumptions.value: the label weight percent and density are for the specific lot; verify against the certificate of analysis

substrate-for-velocity.formula: [S] = Km x f/(1 - f) with f = target_velocity/Vmax; at f = 0.5, [S] = Km; fold_km = f/(1 - f).
substrate-for-velocity.edition: The Michaelis-Menten equation inverted for the substrate concentration at a target fraction of Vmax, by name.
substrate-for-velocity.freeAccess: Standard biochemistry enzyme-kinetics relation solved for the substrate; the assay conditions govern.
substrate-for-velocity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
substrate-for-velocity.editionNote: The Michaelis-Menten hyperbola v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]) inverted for the substrate concentration that reaches a target fraction f of Vmax: [S] = Km x f/(1 - f). At 50% of Vmax [S] = Km (the definition of Km); the required concentration climbs steeply toward saturation (9 x Km at 90%, 99 x Km at 99%), which is why Vmax is approached but never reached and saturating an enzyme takes a large excess. Assumes steady state with substrate far in excess of enzyme, a single substrate, and no cooperativity or inhibition. An analysis aid, not a validated kinetic assay; the actual assay conditions govern.

assumptions.name: Inverse of the forward tile
assumptions.value: [S] = Km f/(1 - f); feeding the result into michaelis-menten with the same Km returns the target fraction of Vmax

assumptions.name: Steady state
assumptions.value: substrate far in excess of enzyme; single substrate, no cooperativity or inhibition

bakers-percentage.formula: Flour = 100%. Ingredient weight = flour x percent / 100; hydration water = flour x hydration% / 100; total dough = sum of all ingredient weights; total formula % = 100 + sum of the other percentages; per-piece = total / pieces.
bakers-percentage.edition: Baker's percentage (baker's math) - the standard bakery / pizzeria dough formulation method; first-principles arithmetic, public domain.
bakers-percentage.freeAccess: Pure arithmetic, public; the flour weight and the per-ingredient percentages are user-supplied.
bakers-percentage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
bakers-percentage.editionNote: First-principles baker's math. Yeast / leaven amount and ferment time are leaven-type, temperature, and schedule specific; salt is typically about 2% of flour. The tile does the weights, not the schedule.

assumptions.name: Flour basis
assumptions.value: total flour is the 100% basis; every percentage is by weight relative to flour

copper-resistance.edition: CRC Handbook material properties; NIST temperature-coefficient values.
copper-resistance.freeAccess: NIST data free at nist.gov; CRC Handbook by name.
copper-resistance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.

assumptions.name: Conductor purity
assumptions.value: annealed copper / 1350-H19 aluminum

transformer-voltage-regulation.formula: cos = pf; sin = sqrt(1 - pf^2) x (leading ? -1 : +1); VR% = load x (%R cos + %X sin) + load^2 x (%X cos - %R sin)^2 / 200.
transformer-voltage-regulation.edition: Transformer voltage-regulation approximation from %R, %X, and load power factor (an IEEE C57 test-report quantity), first-principles; the utility's voltage study governs the actual profile.
transformer-voltage-regulation.freeAccess: The regulation from %R, %X, and power factor is a standard first-principles approximation; %R and %X come from the transformer's IEEE C57 test report.
transformer-voltage-regulation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
transformer-voltage-regulation.editionNote: Transformer voltage-regulation approximation (from %R, %X, and load power factor). VR% = load x (%R cos + %X sin) + load^2 x (%X cos - %R sin)^2 / 200, with sin taking the load's sign (negative for a leading power factor). The nameplate %Z does not by itself give the regulation because it depends on the %R / %X split and the load power factor: a lagging load sags the voltage while a leading (over-corrected or exporting) load can raise it above nominal. The second (quadrature) term is a small correction that grows with the square of loading. This is the terminal regulation, not the full feeder drop -- conductor voltage drop adds to it. A design aid, not the utility's voltage study.

assumptions.name: Impedance split
assumptions.value: regulation uses %R and %X separately, not just %Z; %Z = sqrt(%R^2 + %X^2)

assumptions.name: Power-factor sign
assumptions.value: lagging sin positive (voltage sags), leading sin negative (voltage can rise)

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: terminal regulation only; conductor voltage drop adds on top

corn-yield-estimate.formula: kernels_per_ear = kernel_rows_around x kernels_per_row; bushels_per_acre = ears_per_thousandth_acre x kernels_per_ear / kernel_factor. Ears counted in 1/1000 acre (17.5 ft of 30-in row); kernel_factor = thousands of kernels per 56-lb bushel (~90).
corn-yield-estimate.edition: Pre-harvest corn yield, the yield component (ear-count) method (Purdue / Iowa State University Extension), by name; the harvested and moisture-corrected yield is the real number, and the combine and scale govern.
corn-yield-estimate.freeAccess: The yield component method is public extension-service agronomy; the ear count, kernel rows, kernels per row, and kernel factor are the field's counts.
corn-yield-estimate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
corn-yield-estimate.editionNote: Weeks before the combine runs, an agronomist can estimate a corn field's grain yield from three counts using the yield component, or ear-count, method. First, count the harvestable ears in one-thousandth of an acre, which at the common 30-inch row spacing is a length of 17 feet 5 inches of a single row. Second, on a representative ear, count the number of kernel rows running around the cob. Third, count the kernels along one of those rows; the rows-around times the kernels-per-row gives the kernels on that ear. The estimated bushels per acre is then the ear count times the kernels per ear, divided by a kernel factor that represents the number of kernels, in thousands, that make up a standard 56-pound bushel. That factor is about 90 for average-sized kernels, but it is adjusted according to how the season is finishing: in a good year with large, heavy kernels the factor drops to roughly 75 to 80, which raises the yield estimate, while in a droughty or stressed year with small, light kernels it rises to about 95 to 100, lowering the estimate. As an example, 32 ears with 16 kernel rows of 35 kernels each, at a factor of 90, works out to 32 times 560 divided by 90, or about 199 bushels per acre; a thinner stand of 28 ears averaging 480 kernels per ear estimates roughly 149. The estimate is made more reliable by taking several 1/1000-acre counts at representative spots across the field and by choosing ears that fairly represent the stand rather than the biggest or smallest, and it is least accurate when taken before the kernels have finished filling, between the R5 dent stage and the R6 black-layer stage of maturity. This is a pre-harvest estimate; the actual harvested yield corrected to standard moisture, produced by the crop-yield calculation, is the real number, and the combine yield monitor and the grain scale govern.

assumptions.name: Yield component method
assumptions.value: bu/ac = ears (per 1/1000 acre) x (rows around x kernels per row) / factor; count ears in 17.5 ft of 30-in row

assumptions.name: Kernel factor
assumptions.value: factor = thousands of kernels per 56-lb bushel: ~90 average, 75-80 big kernels (raises estimate), 95-100 small; roughest before R6 black layer

npk-blend.formula: Nutrient recommendation = max(0, crop demand - soil-test credit) for each of N, P2O5, K2O. Three-straight blend: potash (lb/acre) = K2O rec / 0.60; DAP = P2O5 rec / 0.46 (carrying N = DAP x 0.18); urea = max(0, N rec - N from DAP) / 0.46. Total product = rate x acres.
npk-blend.edition: USDA NRCS Agronomy Technical Note ranges and the state Cooperative Extension Service published recommendations (state-keyed) by name.
npk-blend.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
npk-blend.editionNote: Crop nutrient demand is a representative mid-range starting point; the certified soil-test lab report and the state Extension recommendation for your soil and yield goal govern. Default grades: urea 46-0-0, DAP 18-46-0, muriate of potash 0-0-60. Legumes (soybeans, alfalfa) fix their own nitrogen.

assumptions.name: Representative crop demand
assumptions.value: corn 150-60-40, wheat 100-50-30, soybeans 0-45-80 lb/acre N-P2O5-K2O

assumptions.name: Soil-test credit
assumptions.value: subtracted from crop demand, floored at zero

pv-interconnection-busbar.formula: Load-side: sum = main + PV_existing + PV_proposed; limit = 1.20 * busbar (breaker at the opposite end of the busbar from the main, NEC 705.12(B)(3)(2)) or 1.00 * busbar (other load-side position, 705.12(B)(3)(1)); pass when sum <= limit. Supply-side connection (705.11) is ahead of the service disconnect and is not subject to the busbar rule.
pv-interconnection-busbar.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
pv-interconnection-busbar.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Breaker position
assumptions.value: the 120% allowance requires the PV breaker at the opposite end of the busbar from the main
assumptions.source: NEC 2023 705.12(B)(3)(2); the AHJ inspector verifies position at the panel

assumptions.name: Supply-side exemption
assumptions.value: a 705.11 connection ahead of the service disconnect is governed by service-conductor ampacity, not the busbar rule

hand-signals.formula: (reference page; no compute) Crane, excavator, flagger, and aircraft-marshalling hand signals as described (not depicted) by name only. Image reproduction prohibited.
hand-signals.edition: ASME B30.5 (Mobile and Locomotive Cranes) by name; OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC; FAA AC 120-57B (aircraft marshalling).
hand-signals.freeAccess: 29 CFR 1926 free at ecfr.gov. FAA Advisory Circulars free at faa.gov (Regulations & Policies, Advisory Circulars). ASME B30.5 licensed.
hand-signals.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.
hand-signals.editionNote: Single-edition (descriptions only; image reproduction prohibited per ASME B30.5 / FAA copyright).

shotcrete-rebound-quantity.formula: in_place_cy = area_sf x (thickness_in/12) / 27; shot_cy = in_place_cy / (1 - rebound_pct/100); rebound_cy = shot_cy - in_place_cy.
shotcrete-rebound-quantity.edition: Rebound gross-up identity by name (ACI 506 shotcrete practice); first-principles volume arithmetic.
shotcrete-rebound-quantity.freeAccess: The rebound gross-up identity is public shotcrete practice; ACI 506R describes rebound ranges.
shotcrete-rebound-quantity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
shotcrete-rebound-quantity.editionNote: Rebound depends on process and orientation - roughly 5-15% for wet-mix vertical work and 15-30% for dry-mix (gunite) overhead. The value comes from the applicator's field record or the spec, not a constant. Rebound must be cleaned out and never worked back into the section.

assumptions.name: Rebound loss
assumptions.value: 20% default (wet-mix ~5-15%, dry-mix/overhead ~15-30%); the applicator's field record governs

assumptions.name: Volume constant
assumptions.value: 27 ft^3 per cubic yard (exact)

filter-area-for-loading.formula: Required filter area (ft²) = design_flow / target_loading. Backwash flow = backwash_rate × area. Bands: rapid sand 2-5 gpm/ft², high-rate 5-8 gpm/ft².
filter-area-for-loading.edition: Ten States Standards (Recommended Standards for Water Works), Great Lakes - Upper Mississippi River Board of State and Provincial Public Health and Environmental Managers, current edition by name. AWWA B100 / B130 (filter media) by name.
filter-area-for-loading.freeAccess: Ten States Standards licensed; principles free in published water-treatment texts.
filter-area-for-loading.governance: Estimate. Operator of record and primacy agency govern.
filter-area-for-loading.editionNote: Single-edition (Ten States Standards + AWWA filter-design conventions), the loading-rate relation solved for the area: the filter area needed to hold a target loading rate at the design flow, with the backwash flow that area draws and the loading band named.

assumptions.name: Default backwash rate
assumptions.value: 15 gpm/ft² unless user supplies

bulk-density.formula: Bulk density (g/cm³) = dry_weight / volume. Total porosity = 1 − (bulk_density / particle_density), particle density typical 2.65 g/cm³ for mineral soils.
bulk-density.edition: USDA NRCS Soil Survey Manual (SSM) and Soil Quality Indicators by name.
bulk-density.freeAccess: USDA NRCS materials free at nrcs.usda.gov.
bulk-density.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

assumptions.name: Particle density
assumptions.value: 2.65 g/cm³ for mineral soils unless user supplies

assumptions.name: Compaction threshold
assumptions.value: bulk density that restricts root growth, by texture: sand, sandy loam, loam 1.80; silt loam, clay loam 1.75; silty clay loam 1.65; clay 1.47 g/cm³ (root growth already affected at 1.69 sand, 1.63 sandy loam and loam / 1.60 / 1.55 / 1.39)

selective-coordination-screen.formula: fuses: ratio = upstream_rating / downstream_rating, coordinated when ratio >= the family's published minimum, and then to the interrupting rating. breakers: pickup = upstream_rating x instantaneous_multiplier, the low edge of its band = pickup x (1 - tolerance), and coordination holds only up to that low edge (Bussmann, Selective Coordination, 2008: a 400 A breaker at 5x can trip at 2000 x 0.75 = 1500 A).
selective-coordination-screen.edition: Selective coordination screened by device type -- fuses against the manufacturer's published minimum ratio for the family (commonly 2:1), which holds to the interrupting rating, and breakers only up to the low edge of the upstream instantaneous pickup band, above which both devices open. Cited by name; the ratio and the instantaneous setting are the manufacturer's published values and are entered rather than bundled. A screen, never a study: the published time-current curves, a full coordination study, and the engineer of record govern.
selective-coordination-screen.freeAccess: Both screens are comparisons on values the user reads off the manufacturer's published data; no ratio table or time-current curve is reproduced.
selective-coordination-screen.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
selective-coordination-screen.editionNote: Fuses coordinate on a ratio, and the ratio is a published test result for a specific fuse family rather than a general rule of thumb. Within a family, an upstream fuse at or above the published ratio will not open before a downstream one clears, at any fault current up to the interrupting rating, which is why fuses coordinate all the way down and why the ratio table is the whole answer. Circuit breakers fail differently, and understanding how is the point of screening them separately. A thermal-magnetic breaker's instantaneous element trips essentially without delay, so once the fault current exceeds the upstream breaker's instantaneous pickup both devices open and selectivity is lost, no matter how far apart the ratings are. A four-to-one rating spread that looks comfortable coordinates not at all above the pickup. Coordination therefore holds only up to the LOW edge of that pickup band (Bussmann's 400 A breaker at 5x can trip at 1,500 A, not 2,000), and whether that is acceptable depends entirely on the available fault current at the downstream device. The breaker case has three fixes and all are real work: raise the instantaneous setting if the breaker allows it and the downstream equipment survives the longer clearing time, move to a breaker with a short-time delay and no instantaneous -- which raises incident energy, so the arc-flash and coordination requirements genuinely conflict -- or use fuses.

assumptions.name: Fuse ratios are tested
assumptions.value: a published ratio for a specific family, not a general rule; met, it holds to the interrupting rating

assumptions.name: Breakers lose selectivity above pickup
assumptions.value: above the upstream instantaneous pickup BOTH open, whatever the ratio

assumptions.name: The conflict is real
assumptions.value: removing the instantaneous to coordinate raises arc-flash incident energy

pneumatic-cylinder-scfm.formula: extend = pi (bore/2)^2 x stroke; retract = (pi (bore/2)^2 - pi (rod/2)^2) x stroke; volume per cycle = the sum / 1728; compression ratio = (psig + 14.7) / 14.7; SCFM = volume per cycle x cycles per minute x compression ratio x cylinders; compressor hp = SCFM / CFM-per-hp.
pneumatic-cylinder-scfm.edition: Cylinder swept volume from bore, rod, and stroke, and the compression ratio (gauge pressure + 14.7) / 14.7 that converts compressed volume to FREE air, by name. Demand only: no compressor, receiver, piping, or leakage. The compressor manufacturer's rating at the actual discharge pressure, and an air audit of the real system, govern.
pneumatic-cylinder-scfm.freeAccess: Geometry and the ideal-gas pressure ratio on the user's own cylinder dimensions and supply pressure; no manufacturer consumption table is reproduced.
pneumatic-cylinder-scfm.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pneumatic-cylinder-scfm.editionNote: Compressed air is billed in standard cubic feet, which is free air at atmospheric pressure, and a cylinder is filled with compressed air. Every cubic foot of cylinder volume at ordinary shop pressure took just over seven cubic feet of free air to fill, and every cycle throws all of it away through the exhaust port. That factor of seven is the whole reason pneumatics are expensive to run and the reason a shop's compressor always looks smaller than its air demand. The rod side is the part that gets skipped. On the retract stroke the rod occupies part of the bore, so the retract volume is genuinely smaller than the extend volume, and on a large-rod cylinder the difference is substantial: counting both strokes at full bore over-estimates the demand and counting only the extend stroke under-estimates it by nearly half. The pressure lever is real and underused. Because consumption is proportional to the compression ratio rather than to gauge pressure, dropping a supply from 90 psig to 70 psig cuts consumption by about a fifth, which is free money on any application that still makes its force at the lower pressure. This is demand only, and in most real shops the leakage exceeds the productive demand, so an air audit finds more than a cylinder calculation does.

assumptions.name: Standard versus compressed
assumptions.value: SCFM is free air; the compression ratio converts, and forgetting it understates demand about sevenfold at 90 psig

assumptions.name: The rod side is smaller
assumptions.value: the rod displaces part of the bore on retract; counting both strokes at full bore over-estimates

assumptions.name: Leakage is not counted
assumptions.value: in most shops leakage exceeds productive demand; an air audit governs

wsfu-demand.formula: gpm = interpolate(curve, wsfu): piecewise-linear between published [WSFU, GPM] breakpoints for the selected system type (flush tank or flush valve). Flush-valve systems peak higher at low WSFU.
wsfu-demand.edition: Hunter's curve (NBS BMS65, Methods of Estimating Loads in Plumbing Systems) and IPC 2021 Appendix E (Table E103.3(3)) by name; the curve ships as editable breakpoints read from that table.
wsfu-demand.freeAccess: IPC 2021 free read-only at codes.iccsafe.org; NBS BMS65 is public-domain (US government). The bundled curve carries the Table E103.3(3) values as editable breakpoints.
wsfu-demand.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wsfu-demand.editionNote: The bundled flush-tank and flush-valve curves carry the IPC Table E103.3(3) values (Hunter's curve) as editable breakpoints, linearly interpolated between rows. The output is the design demand, not a metered actual.

assumptions.name: Demand curve
assumptions.value: editable [WSFU, GPM] breakpoints per system type, read from IPC Table E103.3(3)

rusle-soil-loss.formula: a_tons_ac_yr = r_factor x k_factor x ls_factor x c_factor x p_factor; site_tons_yr = a_tons_ac_yr x acres.
rusle-soil-loss.edition: RUSLE (Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation) by name - the USDA public-domain method (Agriculture Handbook 703); every factor user-entered.
rusle-soil-loss.freeAccess: RUSLE is USDA public-domain; the factors come from the SWPPP designer or published state guidance the user enters (no isoerodent map or nomograph reproduced).
rusle-soil-loss.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rusle-soil-loss.editionNote: RUSLE is the USDA public-domain replacement for USLE. It estimates long-term average sheet-and-rill loss only, not gully or channel erosion. The cover factor C is the lever a contractor controls with mulch, a blanket, or seed. The permitting AHJ governs the plan.

assumptions.name: Factors
assumptions.value: R (rainfall erosivity), K (soil erodibility), LS (slope length-steepness), C (cover-management), P (support-practice) all user-entered
assumptions.source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 703 / state SWPPP guidance

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: sheet-and-rill loss only; not gully, channel, or streambank erosion

spray-foam-board-feet.formula: board_feet = area_sf x thickness_in; sets = ceil(board_feet x (1 + waste_pct/100) / yield_bd_ft_per_set).
spray-foam-board-feet.edition: Spray-foam board-feet identity by name (area x thickness gives board-feet; sets from board-feet over the per-set yield); first-principles arithmetic.
spray-foam-board-feet.freeAccess: The board-feet arithmetic is public first-principles; the set yield comes from the product's rating.
spray-foam-board-feet.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
spray-foam-board-feet.editionNote: A board-foot is one square foot one inch thick. The set yield comes from the product (closed-cell about 4,800 board-feet, open-cell far more), and both yield less in the field. Temperature and substrate cut the yield. Distinct from insulation-batt-coverage.

assumptions.name: Set yield
assumptions.value: ~4,800 board-feet for closed-cell, far more for open-cell; both less in the field

assumptions.name: Field factors
assumptions.value: temperature and substrate cut the yield below the rated value

trunk-decay-strength.formula: hollow_d = D - 2t; loss_pct = (hollow_d^3 / D^3) x 100; t_over_R = t / (D / 2); concern when t/R < 0.30.
trunk-decay-strength.edition: Hollow-trunk strength-loss screen (Wagener 1963; Smiley & Fraedrich 1992; Mattheck & Breloer t/R; ISA TRAQ), by name.
trunk-decay-strength.freeAccess: The Wagener cube-law loss and the Mattheck t/R rule are published arboricultural results; a qualified arborist and a TRAQ assessment govern.
trunk-decay-strength.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
trunk-decay-strength.editionNote: Strength loss goes as the cube of the hollow-to-diameter ratio, so a trunk can be about two-thirds hollow and keep most of its strength (the loss is small until the hollow is large, then rises sharply); the Mattheck t/R < 0.30 (sound shell below 30% of the radius) is the common concern trigger; an open cavity (a slot) is far weaker than this closed-hollow estimate. A screen, not a tree-risk determination.

assumptions.name: Closed hollow
assumptions.value: the loss estimate assumes a central closed hollow; an open cavity (slot) is far weaker

assumptions.name: Concern trigger
assumptions.value: t/R < 0.30 (sound shell below 30% of the radius) flags escalation to a full TRAQ assessment

fresnel-zone-clearance.formula: r_n(m) = 17.32 sqrt(n d1 d2 / (f_GHz D)), d1/d2/D in km, D = d1 + d2 (17.32 = sqrt(300) from r_n = sqrt(n lambda d1 d2 / D)); recommended clearance = 0.6 x first-zone radius.
fresnel-zone-clearance.edition: The Fresnel zone radius and the 60%-of-first-zone line-of-sight clearance rule, per ITU-R P.526, by name; first-principles diffraction.
fresnel-zone-clearance.freeAccess: The Fresnel-zone geometry is public first-principles physics and ITU-R P.526 is a free ITU download; the frequency and obstruction geometry are the user's link inputs.
fresnel-zone-clearance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
fresnel-zone-clearance.editionNote: The Fresnel zone radius and the line-of-sight clearance a point-to-point radio link needs. Radio energy travels through an ellipsoidal zone around the straight line between antennas, so an obstruction below the sightline still robs signal by diffraction. The first-zone radius at the obstruction is r1 = 17.32 sqrt(d1 d2 / (f_GHz D)), with d1 and d2 the distances (km) from each end to the obstruction and D their sum; it is largest at midspan - a 2.4 GHz 5 km link has a 12.5 m first-zone radius at its midpoint. The industry rule keeps at least 60% of the FIRST Fresnel zone clear of terrain, buildings, and trees (7.5 m here); below that the link loses margin to diffraction even with a nominally clear sightline. Higher zones (n = 2, 3) are reported for reference but the 60%-of-first-zone rule governs. Earth curvature (midpath bulge = D^2/(8kR), R the earth radius, k ~ 4/3) and antenna height are added to the clearance budget separately. A planning geometry; the path survey and a link test govern.

assumptions.name: Fresnel radius
assumptions.value: r_n = 17.32 sqrt(n d1 d2 / (f_GHz D)), km and GHz

assumptions.name: 60% rule
assumptions.value: keep >= 60% of the first (n=1) zone clear; earth curvature and antenna height are separate

fuel-surcharge.formula: FSC/mi = (current - base) / MPG peg when current > base, else 0; total = FSC/mi x loaded miles.
fuel-surcharge.edition: Standard pegged fuel-surcharge identity; DOE/EIA weekly national average diesel index (by name).
fuel-surcharge.freeAccess: DOE/EIA weekly diesel price free at eia.gov.
fuel-surcharge.governance: Math aid for personal verification. The ELD on the truck and the carrier tariff are the legal record. State limits may be lower than federal.
fuel-surcharge.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering-practice / first-principles take-off; refresh as practice and product data shift).

assumptions.name: Index
assumptions.value: DOE/EIA national average unless the contract names another (advisory)

eyring-reverberation.formula: RT60 = 0.049 x V / (-S x ln(1 - a_bar)), a_bar = total_sabins / S = A/S; Sabine RT60 = 0.049 x V / A for comparison.
eyring-reverberation.edition: C.F. Eyring (Eyring-Norris) reverberation equation (J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 1930; public domain); the high-absorption companion to Sabine.
eyring-reverberation.freeAccess: The Eyring-Norris equation is public-domain acoustics; a_bar (the average absorption coefficient) and the surface area are the user's own room take-off, and the 0.049 imperial coefficient is an editable field.
eyring-reverberation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
eyring-reverberation.editionNote: The Eyring-Norris reverberation time RT60 = 0.049 V / (-S ln(1 - a_bar)), where V is the room volume, S the total interior surface area, and a_bar = A/S the average absorption coefficient (total sabins over total surface). It is the form used when the average absorption is high and the Sabine estimate (RT60 = 0.049 V / A) over-predicts: Sabine treats absorption as continuous, while Eyring models it as occurring on each reflection, so Eyring returns a shorter RT60 whenever a_bar exceeds a few tenths -- a 5,000 ft^3 room with 1,300 ft^2 of surface at a_bar 0.30 is 0.53 s by Eyring versus 0.63 s by Sabine. As a_bar approaches zero, -ln(1 - a_bar) approaches a_bar and the two equations converge, so a lightly-treated live room reads nearly the same either way and the gap opens as treatment is added. Use Eyring for studios, control rooms, and heavily-treated spaces; Sabine is the quick estimate for a live room. Frequency-average coefficients hide the band-by-band picture; the acoustician and the venue govern the treatment design.

assumptions.name: Eyring-Norris equation
assumptions.value: RT60 = 0.049 V / (-S ln(1 - a_bar)); reduces to Sabine as a_bar -> 0

assumptions.name: Average absorption
assumptions.value: a_bar = total sabins / total surface area, 0 < a_bar < 1

assumptions.name: When to use
assumptions.value: Eyring for high-absorption (well-treated) rooms; Sabine over-predicts there

flywheel-energy.formula: I = (weight_lb / 32.174) x radius_of_gyration_ft^2; omega = rpm x pi/30; kinetic_energy_ftlb = 0.5 x I x omega^2; speed_fluctuation_pct = 100 x energy_fluctuation_ftlb / (I x omega^2) = 100 x pulse / (2 x KE).
flywheel-energy.edition: Flywheel stored rotational kinetic energy and coefficient of fluctuation (machine-design first principles; Machinery's Handbook flywheel practice), by name; the actual moment of inertia from the flywheel geometry, the load's real energy profile, and the drive and prime mover govern the design.
flywheel-energy.freeAccess: The rotational-energy relation (one-half I omega squared) is public physics; the flywheel weight, radius of gyration, speed, and the load's energy pulse are the machine's values.
flywheel-energy.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flywheel-energy.editionNote: A flywheel smooths out a machine whose torque or load comes in pulses -- a punch press, a shear, a reciprocating engine or compressor -- by storing rotational kinetic energy on the easy part of the cycle and giving it back on the hard part. The stored energy is one-half of the mass moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. In US customary units the moment of inertia, I, is the flywheel's weight divided by the acceleration of gravity, 32.174 feet per second squared, multiplied by the square of the radius of gyration, k. The radius of gyration describes where the mass sits: for a solid disk it is the radius divided by the square root of two, and for a thin rim it is essentially the rim radius, which is why real flywheels concentrate their mass at the outer rim -- a rim stores far more energy per pound than a disk of the same weight and diameter. The angular velocity in radians per second is the rpm times pi divided by thirty. A 100-pound flywheel with a one-foot radius of gyration turning at 1,000 rpm therefore stores one-half times 100 over 32.174 times the square of 1,000 times pi over thirty, or roughly 17,000 foot-pounds of energy. When the driven machine pulls an energy pulse out of the flywheel during a working stroke, the flywheel slows down slightly; the fraction by which its speed swings is the coefficient of fluctuation, which equals the energy fluctuation divided by the product of the inertia and the square of the angular velocity, or equivalently the pulse divided by twice the stored energy. So a 2,000 foot-pound draw on the example flywheel produces a speed swing of about 5.9%. Machines are designed to a target coefficient of fluctuation -- roughly 0.002 for alternating-current generators that need very steady speed, up to about 0.2 for punches and shears where a larger swing is acceptable -- and the flywheel's inertia is increased until the swing meets the target. This is a sizing aid; the actual moment of inertia computed from the real flywheel geometry, the true energy profile of the load over its cycle, and the drive train and prime mover govern the final design.

assumptions.name: Rotational KE
assumptions.value: KE = 1/2 I omega^2; I = (W/g) k^2 (g = 32.174 ft/s^2); k = radius of gyration (disk r/sqrt(2), rim ~ r); omega = rpm x pi/30

assumptions.name: Coefficient of fluctuation
assumptions.value: Cs = energy pulse / (I omega^2) = pulse / (2 KE); target ~0.002 (AC generators) to ~0.2 (punches/shears)

furnace-temp-rise.formula: delta_T = supply_air - return_air; output = input x efficiency / 100; CFM = output / (1.08 x delta_T). Verdict checks delta_T against the rating-plate rise range.
furnace-temp-rise.edition: First-principles sensible-heat relation Qs = 1.08 x CFM x delta-T (public); the 1.08 air factor is fixed; the efficiency (default 80%) is editable.
furnace-temp-rise.freeAccess: The sensible-heat relation is public physics; the rating-plate rise range governs.
furnace-temp-rise.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
furnace-temp-rise.editionNote: Single-edition (the equipment manufacturer's rating plate and the licensed tech govern).

assumptions.name: Air factor
assumptions.value: 1.08 BTU/hr per CFM per F is sea-level standard air; at altitude or high humidity it falls (air-density-correction gives the corrected factor)

assumptions.name: Efficiency
assumptions.value: default 80% steady-state / thermal efficiency, an editable nameplate value

assumptions.name: Rise range
assumptions.value: default 40 to 70 F; the rating plate's stamped range is the governing limit

vfd-energy-savings.formula: vfd_kwh = full_load_kw x (frac_a^3 x hours_a + frac_b^3 x hours_b + frac_c^3 x hours_c); full_kwh = full_load_kw x (hours_a + hours_b + hours_c); saved_kwh = full_kwh - vfd_kwh; saved_usd = saved_kwh x rate_kwh.
vfd-energy-savings.edition: The centrifugal affinity cube law (P / P_full = (Q / Q_full)^3 for a fixed system curve) and the US DOE motor-systems / pump-system energy method, by name; the relations are public.
vfd-energy-savings.freeAccess: The affinity laws and the DOE motor/pump-system energy method are public; the DOE MotorMaster and pump-system tip sheets are free at energy.gov. The arithmetic is public.
vfd-energy-savings.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
vfd-energy-savings.editionNote: The centrifugal affinity laws (P / P_full = (Q / Q_full)^3 for a fixed system curve) and the US DOE motor-systems / pump-system energy method. The cube law holds for a centrifugal pump or fan on a friction-dominated system - a large static-head component flattens the system curve and reduces the savings. The baseline here is full-speed operation for the same hours (a throttled or dampered constant-speed device already saves a little on its own, so the VFD delta versus a throttle is smaller than versus full speed); VFD and motor losses at low speed trim several points off the ideal (DOE Motor Tip Sheet #11: 82.9% saved at half speed where the cube law says 87.5%). A screening estimate, not a metered measurement-and-verification.

assumptions.name: Affinity cube law
assumptions.value: part-flow power scales as the cube of the flow (speed) ratio on a fixed system curve

assumptions.name: Duty cycle
assumptions.value: annual energy is the flow-cubed power summed over the hours in each of three flow bins

assumptions.name: Baseline
assumptions.value: savings are versus full-speed operation for the same hours; friction-dominated system assumed

level-loop-adjustment.formula: misclosure = last_elev - known_close; cum_i = sum(dists[0..i]); correction_i = -misclosure x cum_i / cum_total; adjusted_i = elev_i + correction_i.
level-loop-adjustment.edition: The compass-rule (distance-weighted) distribution of a level-loop misclosure, the vertical analog of the horizontal compass rule, as compiled in the standard surveying references (Ghilani/Wolf, Elementary Surveying), by name.
level-loop-adjustment.freeAccess: The compass-rule adjustment is a public surveying result; FM 5-233 (Construction Surveying) is a public-domain US Government reference.
level-loop-adjustment.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
level-loop-adjustment.editionNote: The compass-rule level-loop adjustment: the misclosure = last computed elevation - known closing elevation is distributed to each turning point as correction = -misclosure x (cumulative distance to the point / total distance), so the correction grows with the distance leveled and the last point takes the full correction and closes exactly on its known elevation, as compiled in the standard surveying references. This is the vertical analog of the horizontal compass rule; it assumes the error accumulates with the length leveled (equal-weight-per-setup is an alternative weighting), the rod readings are already corrected, and the loop is one continuous run. A computational aid; the project survey control and specifications govern.

assumptions.name: Distance weighting
assumptions.value: correction proportional to the cumulative distance leveled to each point; the last point takes the full misclosure and closes exactly

assumptions.name: Single loop
assumptions.value: one continuous level run with corrected rod readings; a network needs a least-squares adjustment

composite-curve-number.formula: Connected (figure 2-3): CNc = CNp + (Pimp/100)(98 - CNp). Unconnected, total impervious under 30% (figure 2-4): CNc = CNp + (Pimp/100)(98 - CNp)(1 - 0.5 R), R = unconnected fraction of the impervious area.
composite-curve-number.edition: The NRCS TR-55 (Urban Hydrology for Small Watersheds, 1986) Chapter 2 composite curve number for impervious area, figures 2-3 and 2-4, by name; verified against TR-55 example 2-4 (CNp 74, 25% impervious, R 0.5 -> CNc 78.5).
composite-curve-number.freeAccess: TR-55 is a free USDA NRCS publication; the connected and unconnected composite-CN equations are published in it.
composite-curve-number.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
composite-curve-number.editionNote: The TR-55 Chapter 2 composite curve number for a developed area with impervious cover, the CN the runoff calculation needs before it can run. Directly connected impervious area (roofs and pavement piped straight to the storm system) uses figure 2-3: CNc = CNp + (Pimp/100)(98 - CNp), blending the pervious CN with the CN 98 of the impervious fraction. Unconnected impervious area (that drains across pervious ground first, so some runoff re-infiltrates) uses figure 2-4: CNc = CNp + (Pimp/100)(98 - CNp)(1 - 0.5 R), where R is the fraction of the impervious area that is unconnected -- which is why disconnecting downspouts onto a lawn lowers the effective CN. Figure 2-4 applies only when the total impervious area is under 30%; above that, treat it as connected. The pervious CN itself (from land cover and hydrologic soil group, Table 2-2) is the user's input. A design aid; the local drainage manual and the engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: Connected impervious
assumptions.value: CNc = CNp + (Pimp/100)(98 - CNp)

assumptions.name: Unconnected impervious
assumptions.value: CNc = CNp + (Pimp/100)(98 - CNp)(1 - 0.5 R), total impervious under 30%

assumptions.name: Pervious CN
assumptions.value: CNp from land cover and hydrologic soil group (user-supplied)

rc-hook-development.formula: psi_c = f'c/15,000 + 0.6 (f'c < 6,000 psi, else 1.0); ldh = (fy psi_e psi_r psi_o psi_c / (55 lambda sqrt(f'c))) db^1.5; ldh = max(ldh, 8 db, 6 in).
rc-hook-development.edition: The ACI 318-19 Eq. 25.4.3.1a hooked-bar tension development length with the 25.4.3.2 modification factors and the max(8 db, 6 in) minimum, by name.
rc-hook-development.freeAccess: ACI 318 is readable free through the ACI online reading room at concrete.org; Eq. 25.4.3.1a and the 25.4.3.2 factor table are in the published code.
rc-hook-development.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rc-hook-development.editionNote: The ACI 318-19 Eq. 25.4.3.1a ldh = (fy psi_e psi_r psi_o psi_c / (55 lambda sqrt(f'c))) db^1.5, the 25.4.3.2 factors (psi_e 1.0/1.2/1.3 for coating, psi_r confining reinforcement, psi_o side cover/location, psi_c = f'c/15,000 + 0.6 for f'c below 6,000 psi), and the max(8 db, 6 in) minimum. This returns the tension development length of a standard 90 or 180 degree hooked deformed bar - it applies the modification factors as entered (defaulting to the base 1.0 values), assumes normalweight concrete unless lambda is set, and does not cover headed bars (25.4.4), compression development, or the hook geometry and bend-diameter detailing. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped detailing.

assumptions.name: Hook equation
assumptions.value: ldh scales with db^1.5 - not linearly - through Eq. 25.4.3.1a

assumptions.name: Modification factors
assumptions.value: psi_e epoxy, psi_r confinement, psi_o location/cover, psi_c strength (f'c/15,000 + 0.6 under 6,000 psi)

assumptions.name: Floor
assumptions.value: never less than 8 bar diameters nor 6 in

assumptions.name: Special moment frame joint (option, added 2026-10-08)
assumptions.value: ldh = fy db / (65 lambda sqrt(f'c)), at least 8 db and 6 in (10 db and 7.5 in lightweight), No. 3-11, no psi factors; a straight bar needs 2.5 ldh, or 3.25 ldh with over 12 in of concrete below. Equation as quoted in PCI Journal, March-April 2024 (Ghosh).

dry-time-projection.formula: remaining_pts = current_mc_pct - goal_mc_pct; days_to_goal = remaining_pts / daily_drop_pct (constant-rate, optimistic near goal). A non-positive daily drop reports 'not progressing' rather than dividing.
dry-time-projection.edition: Linear-trend completion projection, by name; ANSI/IICRC S500. The constant-rate projection is a field-arithmetic identity, not edition-bound.
dry-time-projection.freeAccess: Turns the drying-log readings into a schedule: how many days remain to the dry goal at the observed rate, and a stalled-job flag.
dry-time-projection.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
dry-time-projection.editionNote: Single-edition (the linear projection does not roll). Drying is NON-LINEAR and slows as it approaches the goal, so a constant-rate projection is a planning estimate that runs OPTIMISTIC near the end. The drying-log boundary readings and the restorer's daily monitoring GOVERN the actual endpoint; the dry standard is the unaffected reference, not an absolute number. ANSI/IICRC S500 names the dry standard.

assumptions.name: Constant rate
assumptions.value: the projection assumes the last 24-hour drop continues; real drying slows near the goal

assumptions.name: Dry standard
assumptions.value: the goal is the unaffected reference moisture content, not an absolute number

radiant-loop-sizing.formula: tube_ft = floor_area_ft2 x 12 / spacing_in; loops = ceil(tube_ft / max_loop_ft); per_loop_ft = tube_ft / loops; total_gpm = load_btuhr / (500 x design_dt); per_loop_gpm = total_gpm / loops.
radiant-loop-sizing.edition: First-principles tube-footage, loop-count, and the GPM = Q / (500 x delta-T) hydronic flow relation, by name; the radiant-panel practice per ASHRAE HVAC Systems and Equipment (radiant panel chapter) and the Radiant Panel Association. Not edition-bound.
radiant-loop-sizing.freeAccess: The footage is area over the on-center spacing, the loop count is the footage over the loop limit, and the 500 x delta-T flow constant is the standard water-side relation; all public.
radiant-loop-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
radiant-loop-sizing.editionNote: Single-edition (the geometry and the 500-constant flow relation do not roll). The MANUFACTURER'S TUBING TABLES and the room-by-room heat loss govern the final layout - this sizes footage, loops, and flow from a uniform load, not the panel surface-temperature or downward-loss design. ASHRAE and the Radiant Panel Association name the practice.

assumptions.name: Footage
assumptions.value: one foot of tube per (spacing / 12) ft^2 of floor, a uniform serpentine layout

assumptions.name: Loop limit
assumptions.value: max loop length default 300 ft for 1/2 in PEX; the manufacturer's table governs the actual limit by tube size

assumptions.name: Flow constant
assumptions.value: GPM = Btu/hr / (500 x delta-T), the standard water-side sensible-heat relation

refractory-shell-temperature.formula: one-dimensional steady-state plane-wall conduction: each layer contributes thickness / conductivity and the outer film one / coefficient, the flux is the total temperature drop over the total resistance, and each interface temperature is the hot face less the flux times the resistance ahead of it; the shell is the ambient plus the flux times the film resistance.
refractory-shell-temperature.edition: A steady-state series-resistance solve with every interface reported against its own layer's service limit, and the shell against both a personnel limit and, on flue gas service, an acid dew point. Conductivities are ENTERED because refractory k varies strongly with temperature and with the specific product. It does not address transient heating and dry-out schedules, thermal expansion and joints, corners, arches, penetrations, anchors and the thermal bridge each anchor makes, gas-side convection and radiation, slag or chemical attack, or spalling.
refractory-shell-temperature.freeAccess: A sum of resistances and one division; no manufacturer conductivity table is reproduced.
refractory-shell-temperature.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
refractory-shell-temperature.editionNote: The design lives at the interfaces, not at the shell. INSULATING THE OUTSIDE OF A FURNACE MAKES THE INSIDE HOTTER -- adding an outer layer to cut heat loss raises every interface behind the hot face, because less heat is escaping, and a lining 'improved' that way can put a layer above its service temperature. That failure appears months later as a shell hot spot where the backup has shrunk and opened a path, not at commissioning. A layer's service temperature is a limit on its HOT face, the interface ahead of it, not the cooler one behind. The shell carries two limits pulling opposite ways: a personnel and structural limit that wants it cool, and on flue gas service a floor at the acid dew point, roughly 250 to 300 degF depending on the fuel's sulphur, below which sulphuric acid condenses inside the casing -- so over-insulating a flue gas casing to save energy is a corrosion failure.

assumptions.name: Conductivities are entered
assumptions.value: refractory k varies strongly with mean temperature; one value across a 2,000 degF drop is the largest approximation here

assumptions.name: Outer film
assumptions.value: entered, or computed (added 2026-10-09) for a vertical wall in still air: Churchill-Chu natural convection Nu = [0.825 + 0.387 Ra^(1/6)/(1 + (0.492/Pr)^(9/16))^(8/27)]^2 on the wall height plus gray-body radiation at the shell emissivity, iterated with the shell temperature; reproduces Incropera Example 9.2 (Nu 147)

assumptions.name: One-dimensional and steady state
assumptions.value: no transient, corner, penetration, or anchor bridging

assumptions.name: Not a lining design
assumptions.value: material selection, dry-out, and expansion joints are separate
assumptions.source: the refractory manufacturer and the applicable code

shot-size-residence-time.formula: residence time = (barrel capacity / shot size) x cycle time; the usable shot window is commonly 20 to 65% of barrel capacity (Basilius; Plastics Technology gives 25 to 65%), and the barrel range for a given shot inverts it.
shot-size-residence-time.edition: Shot size and residence time as injection moulding practice states them, with the material's maximum residence ENTERED from the resin supplier's processing data because it is a material property rather than a machine one.
shot-size-residence-time.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
shot-size-residence-time.editionNote: The window has a reason at BOTH ends: below the floor the melt makes too many cycles in a hot barrel, above the ceiling the screw has too little stroke and time to homogenise the charge. The consequence at the low end is what matters -- a long residence is survivable on a polyolefin and a degradation risk on PVC, acetal, polycarbonate and many flame-retardant grades, and degraded parts frequently pass dimensional inspection and fail on properties, so the defect SHIPS. Running a small part on whatever large machine is free is therefore a material decision rather than a scheduling one.

assumptions.name: Maximum residence is entered
assumptions.value: a material property from the resin supplier

assumptions.name: Machine rating basis
assumptions.value: machines are commonly rated in ounces of general-purpose polystyrene

assumptions.name: Average residence
assumptions.value: some material in a screw sits far longer than the average

laundry-dryer-evaporation.formula: water to remove = dry weight x retained moisture fraction; heat = water x about 1,200 BTU/lb / dryer efficiency; exhaust cfm = BTU/hr / (1.08 x temperature rise), where 1.08 = 60 min/hr x 0.075 lb/cu ft x 0.24 BTU/lb-F; makeup air = exhaust; louver free area = cfm / face velocity.
laundry-dryer-evaporation.edition: The evaporation load and airflow relations by name, with the adopted mechanical code and NFPA named for dryer exhaust duct sizing, routing, and lint cleaning access -- cited, not mirrored. The dryer manufacturer's fuel consumption per pound of water governs the energy figure.
laundry-dryer-evaporation.freeAccess: Sensible and latent heat arithmetic; no code table is reproduced.
laundry-dryer-evaporation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
laundry-dryer-evaporation.editionNote: Evaporating water is expensive and mechanical extraction is cheap, and the ratio is roughly ten to one -- which makes retained moisture after extraction the single most consequential number in a laundry's energy bill. Ten points on four thousand pounds of linen is four hundred pounds of water a day that either leaves in the extractor for pennies or leaves in the dryer for dollars. The airflow consequence is the one that causes building problems: 4,000 lb a day at 45% over an eight hour shift is about 3,571 cfm of continuous exhaust and the same 3,571 cfm of makeup the room has to admit -- about 14 sq ft of gross louver at 500 fpm and a 50% free-area fraction. A room with a 4 sq ft transfer grille runs negative and pulls the difference down water heater flues and past every combustion appliance in the mechanical room.

assumptions.name: 1,200 BTU per pound of water
assumptions.value: a working approximation; the dryer's own fuel per pound of water is better

assumptions.name: Makeup air equals exhaust
assumptions.value: the room admits it deliberately or through the building

assumptions.name: Lint is a fire problem, not an airflow one
assumptions.value: duct sizing does not make a duct cleanable
assumptions.source: the adopted mechanical code and NFPA

galvanic-area-ratio.formula: galvanic current = cathodic current density x cathode area; anode current density = that current / anode area; penetration = anode density x electrochemical equivalent / metal density.
galvanic-area-ratio.edition: Potentials measured in the actual service electrolyte; published galvanic series and the materials engineer govern.
galvanic-area-ratio.freeAccess: Public electrochemistry; galvanic series are widely published.
galvanic-area-ratio.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
galvanic-area-ratio.editionNote: The galvanic series tells you which metal corrodes; only the geometry tells you whether anyone will notice. Reversing the area ratio changes the attack by that ratio squared. Coating the anode makes it worse.

assumptions.name: Cathodic limit
assumptions.value: current is set by what the cathode supports

assumptions.name: Electrolyte
assumptions.value: potentials are specific to the service electrolyte and temperature

packaging-yield-loss.formula: packaged = V x (1 - transfer) x (1 - fill); whole packages = floor(packaged / size); remainder = packaged - whole x size.
packaging-yield-loss.edition: Yield bookkeeping; a half barrel is 15.5 gal and a sixth barrel 5.16 gal. The brewery's own packaging records govern.
packaging-yield-loss.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
packaging-yield-loss.editionNote: Remainders do not scale or average, which is why yield is tracked in whole packages rather than percentages.

assumptions.name: Losses
assumptions.value: each as a percentage of the volume entering that step

rack-base-plate-anchorage.formula: Overturning M_o = lateral force x effective height; resisting M_r = 0.6 x frame weight x half the frame depth (ANSI MH16.1 ASD uplift combination); net uplift = (M_o - M_r) / frame depth; anchors = net uplift / allowable tension per anchor, rounded up.
rack-base-plate-anchorage.edition: ANSI MH16.1, the applicable building code and its seismic provisions, and the post-installed anchor's evaluation report at the slab thickness, concrete strength, and edge distance actually present.
rack-base-plate-anchorage.freeAccess: The statics are public; ANSI MH16.1 and anchor evaluation reports are published by their own bodies.
rack-base-plate-anchorage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rack-base-plate-anchorage.editionNote: The anchorage calculation is really a question about the floor. A warehouse slab is routinely thinner, weaker, more cracked, and closer to a joint than the rack drawings assumed, and anchor capacity tables assume otherwise.

assumptions.name: Lateral force
assumptions.value: entered as a coefficient on the frame weight acting at a fraction of the frame height

assumptions.name: Remedies
assumptions.value: a larger plate, a thicker or reinforced slab, a shallower frame, or bracing to the structure -- none is a field decision

ice-melt-working-temperature.formula: ice mass = area x thickness x ice density; product = ice mass / the melting capacity at that temperature; the comparison divides by the capacity at a second temperature.
ice-melt-working-temperature.edition: Published deicer melting capacity and eutectic data. Capacities and the practical working limit are ENTERED laboratory figures: rock salt roughly 46 lb of ice per lb at 30 degF, 8.6 at 20 and under 5 at 10.
ice-melt-working-temperature.freeAccess: A mass calculation and a division by a published capacity.
ice-melt-working-temperature.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ice-melt-working-temperature.editionNote: THE EUTECTIC IS A THERMODYNAMIC BOUNDARY AND THE WORKING LIMIT IS AN OPERATIONAL ONE, and confusing them is the most common error in deicer selection -- for sodium chloride they are more than twenty degrees apart (-6 degF against a practical 15 to 20), and a bag advertising a very low temperature is usually quoting the eutectic. THE CAPACITY COLLAPSE IS THE RESULT: the same 1 in of ice off 1,000 sq ft takes 103 lb of rock salt at 30 degF and 973 at 10, NINE TIMES the material for a twenty degree drop -- and the 10 degF figure is arithmetic rather than practice, because below the working limit the brine refreezes about as fast as it is made and no quantity produces the result. A cold event calls for a DIFFERENT CHEMISTRY, not a heavier application, and spreading heavier is the most common winter operations mistake there is. Calcium chloride's low limit is thermodynamic: it releases heat as it dissolves, and the cost, hygroscopicity and aggressiveness come with it. CAPACITIES ARE LABORATORY FIGURES AND NOT FIELD YIELDS.

assumptions.name: Capacities are laboratory figures
assumptions.value: stated time, temperature and ice thickness; a field application is substantially less effective

assumptions.name: Ice density
assumptions.value: 57.2 lb per cu ft, entered and adjustable

assumptions.name: Working limits are practice ranges
assumptions.value: suppliers differ; they are entered rather than defined

emergency-water-bleach-dose.formula: drops = table rate x gallons (8 drops per gallon of 6%, 6 drops per gallon of 8.25%, other strengths scaled from the 6% row to the same chlorine mass); doubled for cloudy, colored, or very cold water after settling and filtering; teaspoons = drops / 96 at the table's implied 1/96 tsp drop; mL = drops x drop volume; dose mg/L = mL x strength% x 10 / litres of water.
emergency-water-bleach-dose.edition: EPA "Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water" bleach table and procedure (stand 30 minutes, check for a slight chlorine odor, redose and stand 15 minutes more), read at epa.gov on 2026-09-30, and CDC "How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency", both by name. The local health department and the water utility's boil-water or do-not-drink notice govern.
emergency-water-bleach-dose.freeAccess: The EPA and CDC emergency disinfection pages are free public federal guidance; the per-gallon rates are restated and scaled, and the dose is a mass balance on the label strength.
emergency-water-bleach-dose.governance: Estimate. Operator of record and primacy agency govern.
emergency-water-bleach-dose.editionNote: The EPA table is a scaled constant and its per-gallon rate is the whole of it: 8 drops of 6% or 6 drops of 8.25% per gallon, both near 6.5 mg/L. The table is not self-consistent. Every row implies a drop of 1/96 teaspoon except 2 gallons of 6%, printed as 16 drops (1/4 tsp): 16 drops at 1/96 tsp is 1/6 tsp, so measuring the printed teaspoon doses 1.5 times the counted rate, about 9.8 mg/L, which is Ready.gov's 1/8 tsp per gallon. The quart row delivers 8 drops per gallon of 8.25% rather than 6 because a drop cannot be split. The mg/L is a dose, not a residual: chlorine demand from organics, iron, and cold-water kinetics consumes part of it, and the 30-minute smell test is the field check that some free chlorine remains. Bleach does not make chemically contaminated water safe at any dose and does not reliably inactivate Cryptosporidium.

assumptions.name: One drop is 1/96 teaspoon
assumptions.value: about 0.0513 mL, the volume every row of the EPA table implies except the 2 gallon 6% row
assumptions.source: EPA Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water

assumptions.name: Strength read as grams per 100 mL
assumptions.value: the nominal label strength, accurate to roughly 10%; an old bottle delivers less than its label

assumptions.name: Double for cloudy, colored, or very cold water
assumptions.value: applied after settling and filtering, not instead of it
assumptions.source: EPA and CDC emergency disinfection guidance

generator-battery-hybrid-fuel.formula: energy balance (P_g - L) x eta x h = L x (24 - h), so generator hours h = 24 L / (L + (P_g - L) eta); hybrid fuel = h x gph(P_g); continuous fuel = 24 x gph(L), both from the four-point fuel curve; saving = continuous - hybrid; usable battery per cycle = L x (24 - h) / cycles per day.
generator-battery-hybrid-fuel.edition: A first-principles daily energy balance, with fuel read from the manufacturer's four-point fuel curve as in generator-part-load-fuel (worked example from the Cummins C60D6R data sheet D-6567); the generator and battery manufacturers named as governing.
generator-battery-hybrid-fuel.freeAccess: An energy balance and interpolation on figures the user enters from the equipment data sheets; nothing proprietary is reproduced.
generator-battery-hybrid-fuel.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
generator-battery-hybrid-fuel.editionNote: During the ON hours the generator carries the load at an efficient set point and charges the battery with its surplus; during the OFF hours the battery carries the load alone. Surplus stored, less the round-trip loss, equals the energy drawn, which gives the generator hours directly, and the fuel curve converts hours to gallons for both the hybrid and continuous light-load running. The battery is sized per cycle: one long OFF period needs a battery covering most of a day's load, and four shorter ones need a quarter of that, at the cost of more generator starts. The fuel saving does not depend on how the OFF hours are divided. The saving is often modest; the larger benefit is usually mechanical -- the generator never runs in the light-load region where it wet-stacks, and its run hours fall by how far the load sits under the set point (about 60% at the worked 15 kW load, almost nothing near the set point).

assumptions.name: Constant average load
assumptions.value: the day's load is carried at its average; variation through the day is not modelled

assumptions.name: Round-trip efficiency
assumptions.value: the battery returns eta of the surplus stored

assumptions.name: Four-point fuel curve
assumptions.value: gph interpolated at the set point and at the load, flagged below 1/4 load
